blocks.prompt: The Mammal That Flies With Its Hands
blocks.text: A bat is a mammal, just like you. It has fur. It drinks milk from its mom when it is small. But a bat can do one thing no other mammal can do. It can really fly. A bird's wing is covered in feathers. A bat's wing is skin, stretched over long finger bones. When a bat flies, it is flying with its hands. Most bats fly at night. It is dark, so they shout instead of looking. The sound bounces off a moth and comes back. The bat hears the echo and knows just where the moth is.

blocks.prompt: Shouting in the Dark
blocks.text: Stand in a dark room and shout. The sound leaves your mouth, hits the wall, and comes back to your ears as an echo. Now imagine doing that hundreds of times a second, while flying, and using the echoes to build a picture of everything around you. That is what a hunting bat does. Most bats hunt insects at night. A bat sends out short, high squeaks. The squeaks are too high for people to hear. When a squeak hits a moth, a tiny bit of the sound bounces back. From that echo the bat learns where the moth is, how big it is, which way it is going, and how fast. Then the bat turns and takes it out of the air. Scientists call this echolocation. Bats are not blind. Every bat can see. But eyes are not much use in a cave at midnight, and ears are. A little brown bat can catch hundreds of insects in a single hour, all by sound.

blocks.prompt: Flying With Your Hands
blocks.text: Hold your hand up and spread your fingers. Now imagine those fingers stretched until they are longer than your whole arm, with a thin sheet of skin webbed between them. You are looking at a bat's wing. Bats are the only mammals that truly fly. Flying squirrels glide, which is really just falling with style. A bat flaps, climbs, hovers, and turns on a coin. Its scientific group is called Chiroptera, which means hand wing in Greek, and the name is exact. A bat's wing bones are the same bones in your arm and hand: upper arm, forearm, wrist, and four long fingers holding the skin open like the ribs of an umbrella. The thumb stays short and sticks out at the front as a small claw for climbing. Because the wing is skin and not feathers, a bat can change its shape in mid-flight, folding and cupping the surface to steer in ways no bird can copy. The cost is that skin tears. The benefit is that skin heals. This same hand-wing design explains why bats hang upside down. Their legs are thin and light, built for flying rather than standing, so a bat cannot run and launch the way a bird does. Hanging solves it. The bat lets go, drops, and is already flying. Even the grip is free: a tendon in each foot locks the toes shut under the bat's own weight, so a sleeping bat holds on without using any muscle at all.

blocks.prompt: The Night Shift
blocks.text: Every evening, as the light drains out of the sky, a workforce clocks on that almost nobody sees. There are more than 1,400 species of bat. Roughly one in every five kinds of mammal on Earth is a bat, which makes them the second largest group of mammals after the rodents. They are not rodents themselves, and they are not close to them. A bat is more closely related to a horse than to a mouse. Most of them eat insects, and they eat a staggering number. A single colony can clear tons of insects out of the air over a summer. Many of those insects are the moths and beetles that eat corn, cotton, and pecans, which is why researchers have estimated that bats save farmers in the United States billions of dollars every year in crops not lost and pesticide not sprayed. The bats present no invoice. Other bats work a different shift. Nectar-feeding bats pollinate agave, which is the plant tequila is made from. Fruit bats carry seeds far out over cleared land and drop them, which is how a burned patch of rainforest starts growing back. Some plants have shaped themselves entirely around bats: flowers that open only at night, pale enough to find in the dark, on stalks strong enough to hold a hanging visitor. The insect side of this has been an arms race for about 50 million years. Bats hunt by shouting and listening to the echoes, so certain moths evolved ears tuned precisely to bat calls. Hear a hunting bat, and the moth folds its wings and drops out of the sky. Bats answered by shifting their calls to frequencies those ears miss. Tiger moths went further still. When a bat closes in, they click back, and those clicks jam the bat's sonar so badly that the strike misses. None of it is guaranteed to continue. Since 2006, a fungus that causes white-nose syndrome has swept across North America, waking hibernating bats over and over through the winter until they burn their fat reserves and starve before spring. Millions have died. Some species have lost more than ninety percent of their numbers. Bats are slow to recover, because most raise a single pup a year. The night shift is quieter than it used to be.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Chiroptera: cheir hand, pteron wing
The wing has more than two dozen joints
Terminal buzz: up to 200 pulses a second
Calls can top 120 decibels at close range
A middle-ear muscle mutes each shout
Moth ears tuned to almost nothing but bat calls

blocks.prompt: Hand Wing: How a Mammal Learned to Hunt With Sound
blocks.text: Start with the name. The scientific order that contains every bat on Earth is Chiroptera, from the Greek cheir, hand, and pteron, wing. It is not a poetic flourish. Open a bat's wing and you find your own skeleton, redrawn: upper arm, forearm, wrist, and four fingers pulled out to absurd lengths, with a living membrane of skin stretched between them. The thumb stays short and clawed, hooked over the front edge for climbing. When a bat flies, it is not flapping a feathered blade the way a bird does. It is swimming through the air with two enormous webbed hands. That difference matters more than it sounds. A bird's wing is a fairly rigid airfoil. A bat's wing is a controllable surface with more than two dozen independent joints in it, laced with muscle and threaded with sensory hairs that report airflow back to the brain. A bat can cup, twist, and reshape each wing separately, in the middle of a single stroke. That is why bats can hover, reverse, and turn inside their own body length, and why a moth being chased by one is in serious trouble. The tradeoff is fragility, because the membrane tears. The compensation is that it heals, quickly and completely, in a way most mammal tissue does not. The second invention is stranger. Most bats hunt in total darkness by making sound and reading its echoes, a process called echolocation. The bat emits a short ultrasonic pulse, far above the ceiling of human hearing, and listens for what comes back. The delay tells it distance. The difference between the two ears tells it direction. The shifting pitch of the returning echo, stretched or squeezed by the target's movement, tells it speed. As the bat closes in it fires faster and faster, up to two hundred pulses a second in the final moment, a burst so rapid that researchers call it the terminal buzz. The bat is refreshing its picture of the moth two hundred times a second while flying at full speed. There is a problem with shouting to see, and it is that shouting is loud. A hunting bat's call can exceed 120 decibels at close range, comparable to a jet engine, and the bat's own ears sit a few centimeters from its mouth. It solves this by contracting a muscle in its middle ear a fraction of a second before each pulse, deafening itself briefly, then relaxing in time to hear the echo return. It does this hundreds of times a second without losing the beat. Evolution rarely leaves such a weapon unanswered. Several families of moth independently evolved ears tuned to almost nothing except the frequencies of bat calls. A moth that hears a distant bat turns and flees. A moth that hears a close one folds its wings and drops. Some bats countered by moving their calls above or below the band those ears cover, hunting in what researchers call an acoustic blind spot. Tiger moths escalated again, answering an incoming bat with rapid clicks of their own that smear the returning echo and make the strike miss. This exchange has been running for roughly fifty million years, and neither side has won. Which makes the present moment grim. In 2006, a cold-loving fungus reached caves in New York and began killing hibernating bats by rousing them repeatedly through the winter until they starved. White-nose syndrome has since killed millions across North America, and several once-common species have declined by more than ninety percent. Bats reproduce slowly, usually one pup a year, so these are not losses that fill back in. One recent study tracked what happened in farm counties after their bats collapsed, and found that insecticide use rose sharply. The animal doing the work was invisible until it stopped.
